topic: Greenhouse gases and UK climate evidence
summary: Climate is the usual weather over many years. Human actions add gases that trap more heat. Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air. This strengthens the greenhouse effect and warms Earth. This does not mean each year or each place gets warmer in a straight line. We can use climate evidence to check changes over time.

cards.title: Burning fuels
cards.text: Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air.
cards.reason: It adds a greenhouse gas. This can strengthen the greenhouse effect.

cards.title: Removing forests
cards.text: Fewer trees can mean less carbon dioxide is taken from the air. Clearing forests can also release stored carbon.
cards.reason: Loss of forest can increase the amount of greenhouse gas in the air. Not every forest fire has the same cause.

cards.title: Farming and gas
cards.text: Some farming adds methane to the air. Methane is a greenhouse gas.
cards.reason: Methane can strengthen the greenhouse effect. Avoid blaming a person or claiming all farming has equal effects.

cards.title: Warmer conditions
cards.text: More trapped heat raises Earth's long-term mean temperature.
cards.reason: Warming is an effect of the strengthened greenhouse effect. It can then contribute to other effects.

cards.title: Rising seas
cards.text: Melting ice on land adds water to the sea. Warm sea water also expands. Sea level can rise.
cards.reason: Both land-ice loss and warming water contribute to rising sea level. Floating sea ice is not the same as ice on land.

cards.title: Heat and heavy rain
cards.text: Warmer conditions can bring more hot spells. Warmer air can hold more water, which can make heavy rain more intense.
cards.reason: Risks vary across places. This does not mean every place gets more rain, or that one event is caused only by climate change.

One cause and effect chain

More carbon dioxide in the air.

The gas is not a lid. Heat still leaves Earth, but more is kept in the climate system.
image_text.Enquiry_Guide.png:
A careful enquiry
1 Read a cause card. Find an effect.
2 Link the steps. Use more gas and more trapped heat.
3 Read the UK graph. Check the year and the unit.
4 Name the highest and lowest selected point.
5 Make a careful link for a general UK region.
This is UK data. It is not a measured local trend or a forecast.

model: I read C1. Burning fuel adds gas to the air. I put it with causes. More gas can trap more heat, so Earth warms. I then read the UK graph. 2025 is the highest selected point. The graph shows selected years, not all years. It does not prove the cause on its own.

evidence.source_institution: Met Office National Climate Information Centre
evidence.source_title: Monthly seasonal and annual mean air temperature for UK
evidence.dataset: HadUK-Grid 1 km land-surface areal series, annual column
evidence.quantity: Annual mean air temperature across the UK
evidence.baseline: None: absolute annual mean temperature, not an anomaly.
evidence.selection_rule: Years at ten-year intervals from 1980 through 2020, followed by the latest complete year 2025.
graph_requirements: Title says Selected UK years; do not imply every intervening year is plotted.
Year axis needs proportional spacing: 2020 to 2025 is half of a ten-year gap.
Temperature axis should begin at zero for a bar chart or clearly label a cropped line-chart axis. Recommended dot/line plot 0 to 12 C with usable labels.
Show points and units; provide the exact table alongside if plotting rounded tenths.
No extrapolation to 2027; 2026 incomplete in the snapshot.
Annual values vary. 2010 is cooler than 2000 in this selection. A cold year does not disprove long-term warming.
This selected-year graph does not alone establish the cause of warming; use checked greenhouse-gas evidence separately.

supporting_sources_no_urls.title: Causes of climate change
supporting_sources_no_urls.facts: Human activities raise greenhouse gas levels. Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide; the enhanced greenhouse effect warms the planet. Natural variability occurs but does not explain the main recent warming.

supporting_sources_no_urls.title: Effects of climate change
supporting_sources_no_urls.facts: UK winters are projected to be warmer and wetter on average; summers hotter and more often drier. Cold or wet seasons can still occur. Effects and preparedness differ across places.

region_sentence_options: For our UK region, warmer conditions can mean we need to plan for hot spells.
For our UK region, warmer conditions and heavier rainfall can affect health, water and places; the risks vary.
evidence.region_scope_caution: Use UK country scale, with our region explicitly a general UK region. Do not name or infer the school's town, county or local area; do not claim a national average is a measured local trend.
